item.title: Airline sets booking record
item.description: FIJI Airways recorded more than 14,000 bookings on September 2, its highest single-day total in the airline’s 75-year history. The figure surpassed the previous record set in 2023 and was recorded during the airline’s global 75th Anniversary Sale.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI Airways recorded more than 14,000 bookings on September 2, its highest single-day total in the airline’s 75-year history.

The figure surpassed the previous record set in 2023 and was recorded during the airline’s global 75th Anniversary Sale.

Fiji Airways managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the result reflected continued demand for travel to Fiji.

“This is our best booking day ever,” Mr Scurrah said.

The booking record comes as Fiji’s tourism sector continues to grow.

Fiji Bureau of Statistics data shows 105,791 visitors arrived in Fiji in July, the first month in which arrivals exceeded 100,000.

Visitor arrivals for the year to July were 4.3 per cent higher than during the same period in 2025.

Business-class bookings were 17 per cent higher on September 2 than on the same day last year, while group bookings nearly doubled.

Fiji Airways has also expanded its network, recently adding the Gold Coast to its Australian schedule. New services to Nouméa, New Caledonia, are scheduled to begin later this month.

The national airline carries a significant share of visitors travelling to Fiji and is a major employer in the country.

Mr Scurrah said the increase in bookings would support activity across the tourism sector.

item.title: Workshop reviews waste sector target
item.description: FIJI’s waste sector accounts for about 9.7 per cent of the country’s total greenhouse gas emissions, prompting the Government to strengthen systems for measuring and monitoring emissions. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change held a Waste Sector Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) Targets, Mitigation Measures and Monitoring Workshop at the University of the South Pacific’s Statham Ca
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’s waste sector accounts for about 9.7 per cent of the country’s total greenhouse gas emissions, prompting the Government to strengthen systems for measuring and monitoring emissions.

The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change held a Waste Sector Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) Targets, Mitigation Measures and Monitoring Workshop at the University of the South Pacific’s Statham Campus on Thursday.

The workshop brought together representatives from government ministries, development partners, municipal councils and other stakeholders to review waste sector targets under Fiji’s NDC 3.0.

Methane from landfills, wastewater treatment facilities, industries and farms are among the sources contributing to emissions from the sector.

Director of Climate Change Senivasa Waqairamasi said stronger action in the waste sector could provide direct benefits to communities.

A key focus was strengthening Fiji’s Monitoring, Reporting and Verification framework to improve the measurement of emissions reductions and track the effectiveness of mitigation measures.

Participants reviewed proposed monitoring protocols and indicators, including institutional responsibilities and procedures for collecting and sharing data.

The initiative is supported by the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, the Center for Clean Air Policy and ImplementaSur.

The improved monitoring system will support implementation of Fiji’s NDC 3.0 waste-sector targets and help guide future climate investment and policy decisions.

item.title: Process exposes 13 ghost officers
item.description: EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro has confirmed that 13 officers were identified as ghost employees following a payroll verification exercise by the Ministry of Education. The exercise was conducted in response to recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report concerning former ministry employees who continued to receive salaries during the 2024 financial year.
item.content:encoded:
EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro has confirmed that 13 officers were identified as ghost employees following a payroll verification exercise by the Ministry of Education.

The exercise was conducted in response to recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report concerning former ministry employees who continued to receive salaries during the 2024 financial year.

Mr Radrodro said payroll verification was an established process to ensure employment records were accurate and public funds were paid only to legitimate employees.

The exercise also resulted in the cessation of salaries for 134 officers in Pay 18/2026 after the ministry identified outstanding permanent appointment documentation.

The affected teachers had been issued permanent appointment contracts through the Fiji Education Management Information System (FEMIS) in 2025 but had not returned signed contracts for processing and updating of employment records.

Mr Radrodro said the teachers continued to receive salaries until Pay 18/2026 despite the required documentation remaining outstanding.

The verification also identified other employment discrepancies. In one case, a former teacher whose contract expired on January 26, 2025, continued receiving salary payments until Pay 18/2026 after leaving the ministry.

The exercise further found that some affected teachers had not renewed their Fiji Teachers Registration Authority (FTRA) licences as required under the FTRA Act.

Mr Radrodro urged officers to complete and return mandatory employment documents and maintain valid FTRA licences.

He also advised employees to raise employment matters through established ministry channels rather than social media.

Mr Radrodro reminded officers of their obligations under the Civil Service Code of Conduct.

item.title: Survey: 76% of young men back wife ‘discipline’
item.description: SEVENTY-SIX per cent of men aged 18 to 35 believe a husband has the right to “discipline” his wife, compared with 59 per cent of older men, the 2025 SCORE survey has found. The survey also found that 57 per cent of young women shared the view, highlighting concerns over the continued acceptance of violence among younger generations.
item.content:encoded:
SEVENTY-SIX per cent of men aged 18 to 35 believe a husband has the right to “discipline” his wife, compared with 59 per cent of older men, the 2025 SCORE survey has found.

The survey also found that 57 per cent of young women shared the view, highlighting concerns over the continued acceptance of violence among younger generations.

Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran said the findings demonstrated the importance of addressing harmful attitudes early, particularly among adolescent boys and young men.

She made the remarks at the Pacific Islands Health Research Symposium High-Level Dialogue at Fiji National University’s Nasinu Campus.

The Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection has developed a Gender-Based Violence Community Awareness Manual to support prevention work in communities.

Ms Kiran said the manual provided culturally responsive guidance for discussions on respectful relationships, early intervention and harmful gender norms. It was also being used to encourage community conversations and promote zero tolerance of gender-based violence.

She said preventing violence required greater attention to the home, where children developed attitudes and behaviours that could shape their relationships later in life.

Positive, non-violent parenting was critical, she said, warning that children exposed to violent discipline could come to regard aggression as normal.

The ministry has begun targeted programs with adolescent boys to challenge harmful attitudes during their formative years.

Ms Kiran said early intervention was needed to prevent these attitudes from becoming entrenched, with the ministry also working with faith-based organisations, including Caritas Fiji.

item.title: Men urged to step up
item.description: MEN from across Suva and Ovalau gathered yesterday in Nabua to discuss how they can play a greater role in addressing social challenges affecting their families and communities. The Men’s Archdeaconry Rally, held at St Matthew’s Anglican Church, brought together almost 100 men from grassroots communities across Suva and Ovalau.
item.content:encoded:
MEN from across Suva and Ovalau gathered yesterday in Nabua to discuss how they can play a greater role in addressing social challenges affecting their families and communities.

The Men’s Archdeaconry Rally, held at St Matthew’s Anglican Church, brought together almost 100 men from grassroots communities across Suva and Ovalau.

Assistant Minister in the Office of the Prime Minister Sakiusa Tubuna, who was a key speaker at the rally, said the gathering provided an opportunity for men to discuss challenges affecting their communities and consider how they could contribute to addressing them.

“Men need to be discussing these issues, and of course the church also plays a very important role,” he said.

“Issues like teenage pregnancy, HIV and AIDS, drugs and the role of men which are affecting families and churches, it all needs greater discussion.”

Mr Tubuna said the Government was also calling on churches to be active in addressing social challenges faced by communities.

He said men did not always take such issues seriously, which was why the rally was organised to bring them together to discuss their role in addressing the problems.

The rally also encouraged Indo-Fijian and non-iTaukei communities to participate and share their views.

“It also promotes and enhances social cohesion between different ethnic communities.”

He said the gathering was more organised than previous rallies and provided an opportunity to look beyond the spiritual aspects of church life and discuss issues affecting families.

Among the ways forward, Mr Tubuna said families should hold regular meetings to discuss issues affecting them.

item.title: ‘Sex stigma may mask HIV spread’
item.description: SEX stigma may be obscuring how HIV is spread in Fiji, as some people may be more willing to report injecting drug use than sexual contact. Rainbow Pride Foundation acting chief executive Asaeli Sinusetaki said the stigma could affect information collected from people living with HIV and, consequently, how authorities understand the country’s growing HIV problem.
item.content:encoded:
SEX stigma may be obscuring how HIV is spread in Fiji, as some people may be more willing to report injecting drug use than sexual contact.

Rainbow Pride Foundation acting chief executive Asaeli Sinusetaki said the stigma could affect information collected from people living with HIV and, consequently, how authorities understand the country’s growing HIV problem.

“There’s more stigma to sex than to drugs,” Mr Sinusetaki said.

He said people could face uncomfortable questions when reporting sexual contact as the likely source of their infection, including questions about their partners.

“How did you get it? Sex. Well, with who?”

Mr Sinusetaki said information gathered through the Moonlight Clinic’s outreach and testing activities indicated that unsafe sex was occurring at significant levels.

However, he said, stronger evidence was needed to establish the main drivers of HIV transmission rather than relying solely on information provided by individuals.

An Integrated Biological and Behavioural Surveillance (IBBS) study is being rolled out to provide that evidence.

The study combines HIV testing and other biological data with information about people’s behaviour and potential risk factors.

Mr Sinusetaki said the approach would help health authorities examine not only the number of people infected but also the behaviours and circumstances associated with HIV transmission.

He said the surveillance would begin in Lautoka before expanding to Suva and other parts of Fiji.

The aim is to identify the major factors contributing to the spread of HIV and strengthen the evidence base for prevention and response measures.

item.title: EDITORIAL COMMENT | We need the truth to fight HIV
item.description: Fiji cannot afford to fight HIV with incomplete information. The suggestion that stigma around sex may be influencing how people report the possible source of their HIV infection should concern all of us.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji cannot afford to fight HIV with incomplete information.

The suggestion that stigma around sex may be influencing how people report the possible source of their HIV infection should concern all of us.

If people feel safer saying they contracted HIV through drug use than through sexual contact, the information collected by health authorities may not fully reflect what is happening in our communities.

This is not about judging people for how they live, who they have sex with or whether they use drugs.

It is about understanding the reality of HIV transmission so that prevention efforts can reach the people who need them most.

Sex remains a difficult subject in Fiji.

Conversations about sexual behaviour can be uncomfortable in families, schools, workplaces and even healthcare settings.

People may fear being judged, shamed or exposed.

That fear can become a barrier to honest disclosure — and when people are not comfortable telling the truth, the picture we build from the available data can become distorted.

That is why the rollout of the Integrated Biological and Behavioural Surveillance study is important.

Testing alone tells us how many people are infected.

Understanding behaviour, circumstances and potential risk factors can help explain why infections are occurring and where prevention efforts need to be strengthened.

Starting the surveillance in Lautoka before expanding to Suva and other parts of Fiji should provide a broader picture of the national situation.

But collecting better data is only one part of the solution.

People must feel safe enough to provide honest information.

Healthcare workers and researchers need to create environments where sensitive questions can be answered without fear of humiliation, discrimination or unnecessary exposure.

Confidentiality must not simply be promised; it must be protected.

We cannot educate people about HIV effectively if we are afraid to talk openly about sex.

Accurate information, testing, treatment, prevention and honest conversations do.

Fiji should therefore welcome evidence that challenges assumptions rather than evidence that confirms what we think we already know.

If the IBBS study shows that sexual transmission is a major driver, we must be prepared to say so clearly.

If it identifies other significant factors, those findings must receive the same attention.

The priority should not be protecting social sensitivities.

Understanding how HIV is actually spreading is the first step towards stopping it.

To do that, Fiji needs data people can trust — and a society in which people feel safe enough to tell the truth.

item.title: Ravunawa: Privacy needed for HIV testing
item.description: THE number of HIV cases recorded in the North may not reflect the true scale of infections, with stigma and fear of being identified potentially discouraging people from coming forward for testing. This has raised concerns over the location of the North’s HIV testing and treatment hub, which is currently based within the Nasea Health Centre in Labasa.
item.content:encoded:
THE number of HIV cases recorded in the North may not reflect the true scale of infections, with stigma and fear of being identified potentially discouraging people from coming forward for testing.

This has raised concerns over the location of the North’s HIV testing and treatment hub, which is currently based within the Nasea Health Centre in Labasa.

Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa said having the service within a health facility could discourage some people from seeking testing because of the stigma surrounding HIV.

“It can indeed discourage some people from visiting the hub,” he said.

Mr Ravunawa said the ministry had received a proposal from the divisional medical officer for additional space at Nasea to accommodate the service.

“We have received the proposal from DMON about the need for space at Nasea.”

He said the proposal was currently awaiting consideration and approval from the Finance Ministry.

“We are also waiting for the Ministry of Civil Service for their approval of the proposed office space.”

He said the proposed office space in Labasa Town would provide an alternative location for HIV-related services and could offer greater privacy to people accessing testing and treatment.

Official Ministry of Health figures recorded 225 laboratory-confirmed positive HIV tests in the Northern Division in 2025, while 84 new cases were registered.

However, UNAIDS has reported that diagnoses may not capture everyone living with the virus.
